metadata.title: FBI says US has seized $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Binance

sources.news_title: FBI says U.S. has seized $1.2B worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Binance
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The FBI said Thursday that it had seized more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange.
The theft of about $6.3 billion from Binance is regarded as the biggest crypto heist in history, and the FBI has previously attributed it to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor. The U.S. government and private sector have so far combined to freeze more than $2.7 billion of the stolen funds, and the Justice Department said Thursday that it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that total.
Typically in those situations, the U.S. government will file a claim of forfeiture with a judge, who will then determine who has a legitimate claim to the recovered funds.
Also Thursday, the FBI blamed North Korea for a separate social engineering scheme that officials say resulted in the theft of $400 million worth of cryptocurrency over the last 18 months. That scheme, known as FaceStealer, involves a complicated chain of events combining the hijacking of popular messaging apps and the recording of deepfake videos.
U.S. officials have repeatedly accused North Korea of using cyber schemes to generate funds for its regime, including its illicit weapons program.

sources.news_title: US seizes North Korean hacking infrastructure, $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance
sources.text:
US seizes North Korean hacking infrastructure, $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance
The Justice Department on Thursday announced coordinated actions against North Korean groups’ campaigns that have stolen billions of dollars in cryptocurrency, seizing cloud infrastructure behind a social engineering scheme known as FaceStealer and the court-authorized seizure of more than $1.2 billion stolen from cryptocurrency exchange Binance.
The larger of the two operations is tied to the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets from Binance, which the FBI has attributed to North Korean military hackers it calls TraderTraitor. Investigators working with private virtual asset service providers have frozen more than $2.7 billion of the stolen funds, and courts have authorized the seizure of more than $1.2 billion of that amount.
A. Tysen Duva, the assistant attorney general in charge of the DOJ’s Criminal Division, said its computer crime section and partners froze the stolen Binance assets “before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” halting “about half of this historic breach.”
The FBI also issued an alert Thursday that detailed the scheme’s mechanics. Hackers known publicly as Sapphire Sleet, BlueNoroff, APT38 and Stardust Chollima hijack accounts on Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord and invite targets to video meetings. Links lead to typo-squatted domains, hosting imposter versions of Zoom and Microsoft Teams “designed by the hackers to be indistinguishable from the genuine interfaces.”
The infrastructure seized by the FBI contained a library of more than 900 secretly recorded webcam videos that the hackers played to impersonate victims in follow-on attacks. The footage was captured from victims as they waited for video chats to begin. The alert published redacted and blurred examples of the library. Because each compromise yields the next victim’s video and contact lists, the pool of targets and victims “grows exponentially,” the alert warned.
The campaign has drained more than $400 million from the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors over the past 18 months. The FBI said it has seized more than 900 victim videos used to impersonate victims in follow-on attacks.
Patrick Grandy, the assistant director in charge of the FBI’s Los Angeles field office, said the scheme is “capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user.”
“It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships,” he said.
The alert also showed the scheme’s reach beyond its direct victims, showing how it was used earlier this year to lure the maintainer of a significant open-source JavaScript library into a fake Teams meeting. Hackers then used the maintainer’s access to create malicious dependencies that could have been downloaded alongside legitimate ones.
For years, North Korea has committed cryptocurrency heists alongside the regime’s expansive scheme to get remote IT workers hired at U.S. businesses, ultimately to launder ill-gotten money and evade economic sanctions. 
Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, told CyberScoop that even with the law enforcement actions, there has been a “significant evolution in both the scale and sophistication” of North Korean schemes.
“While the tactics continue to evolve, the goal remains the same,” Moore told CyberScoop. “They’re exploiting trust to lower a target’s guard and convince them to take an action that leads to compromise. That’s what makes operations like this so effective and why efforts to disrupt them are so important.”
“Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” said Bill Essayli, a U.S. attorney for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”
The FBI credited the cybersecurity firms Arctic Wolf, Jumpsec and Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center for assisting in the investigation and seizure.

‘FaceStealer’ scam tied to $400M+ theft, 900+ webcam recordings
The US government on Thursday said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain use of over $1.2 billion stolen during last month’s $6.3 billion Binance heist, as part of a larger effort to disrupt North Korea’s ongoing cryptocurrency theft.The court also allowed the takedown of cloud-based infrastructure used in a Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) social engineering scheme called “FaceStealer” that has amassed more than $400 million in the last 18 months.It’s called FaceStealer because it involved secretly recorded webcam videos. Victims are typically people working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, along with open source software developers and maintainers who DPRK hackers target in the hope of accessing the software repositories they control as the first step towards creating supply chain attacks.
900+ faces stolen
The FBI said it had seized more than 900 webcam videos belonging to these tech workers.Here’s how the attack works.First, the North Koreans send targets an invitation to join a video meeting. Those invitations come from hijacked accounts that the next intended victim may find familiar or credible.“You’re going to think it’s real because it’s going to be based on either conversations or interests you’ve expressed in the past with this actual person,” said special agent Jeremy Robertson, who oversees counterintelligence and cyber investigations at FBI Los Angeles.“They’re going to then send you a link to catch up, and it’s usually a calendar invite, and it’s going to have some typo-squatted URLs in there,” he told reporters on Thursday.The URL directs the victim to a fake Zoom or Teams meeting, and the cybercriminals record the target’s webcam video while playing a phony, prerecorded video of the person who purportedly sent the meeting invite.Sometimes the hackers also use deepfake videos of well-known individuals in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries, we’re told.“When you log in, whoever invited you – your friend or business associate – is going to be on the screen, but you’re not going to hear any audio,” Robertson said. “But you’re going to see their face, you’re going to see them looking around, you’re going to see them mouthing some words, and then in the text box you’re going to receive some instructions.”
‘You’re on mute’ as a social engineering vectorThe text box tells the victim that the person on the other end of the video call can’t hear them, they need to upgrade their software for the audio to work properly, and it sends a link to the supposed fix.Clicking to access the “fix” installs cryptocurrency-stealing malware on the victim’s computer and sends their contact list to the digital thieves to perpetuate the scam.The FBI attributes FaceStealer to a North Korea-linked group tracked as Sapphire Sleet, which is widely regarded as a Lazarus Group offshoot. Sapphire Sleet is also known as UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff.“The actors behind this activity, commonly referred to as Sapphire Sleet and other associated names, are part of a broader North Korean effort to generate revenue for the regime, to steal virtual assets, and gain access to networks and trusted online ecosystems,” Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI’s Cyber Division, told reporters. “North Korean hackers are increasingly blending cyber intrusion, social engineering, and emerging technologies such as deep fakes to make their impersonation efforts more convincing and scalable.”Binance heist updateThe FBI also provided an update on its efforts to recover the stolen assets from the October 29 attack on Binance. The agency previously blamed the $6.3 billion heist on TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation also linked to Lazarus Group.Last week, Binance revealed the attackers laid the groundwork for their “sophisticated, multi-stage campaign” back in June, and said it involved social engineering during fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method.”  
Since the theft, federal investigators and private-sector partners have helped freeze more than $2.7 billion in stolen assets. The Justice Department’s court authorization covers more than $1.2 billion of that haul.®
